questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the anticoagulant orders for three patients. Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A patient started on oral warfarin today will not have the full effect for [[1]], and the nurse follows the [[2]] to monitor it.

A patient on an unfractionated heparin infusion is monitored with the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) and the [[3]].

A patient taking enoxaparin injections at home usually needs no routine clotting test, but the nurse watches [[4]] because the drug is cleared by the kidneys.

options.text: about 1 hour
options.rationale: This fits a fast drug. Heparin given IV acts immediately; warfarin does not.

options.text: several days
options.rationale: Warfarin works slowly by lowering production of the vitamin K dependent clotting factors, so the full effect takes several days.

options.text: within a few hours
options.rationale: Enoxaparin acts within hours. Warfarin has to wait for the existing clotting factors to be used up.

options.text: the first dose
options.rationale: Oral anticoagulant in this group reaches full effect with the first warfarin dose.

options.text: D dimer
options.rationale: D dimer shows that a clot is being broken down; it does not monitor an anticoagulant.

options.text: aPTT
options.rationale: aPTT measures the intrinsic pathway and monitors heparin, not warfarin.

options.text: platelet count
options.rationale: A platelet count shows bleeding risk from low platelets but does not measure warfarin's effect.

options.text: INR
options.rationale: PT/INR measures the extrinsic pathway and monitors warfarin.

options.text: D dimer
options.rationale: D dimer shows a clot is breaking down; it is not a heparin safety check.

options.text: platelet count
options.rationale: Heparin can lower the platelet count, so platelets are monitored along with the aPTT during heparin therapy.

options.text: hemoglobin
options.rationale: Hemoglobin can show blood loss, but the paired heparin safety check is the platelet count.

options.text: INR
options.rationale: INR monitors warfarin, not heparin.

options.text: liver enzymes
options.rationale: Liver enzymes are not the key enoxaparin check; the drug is cleared by the kidneys.

options.text: kidney function
options.rationale: Enoxaparin is cleared by the kidneys, so kidney function is monitored along with bleeding and platelet counts.

options.text: INR
options.rationale: INR measures warfarin; it does not measure enoxaparin.

options.text: blood glucose
options.rationale: Blood glucose has no link to enoxaparin dosing or safety.

questions.takeaway: Warfarin is slow and is monitored with INR. Heparin is monitored with the aPTT and the platelet count. Enoxaparin usually needs no routine clotting test, but bleeding, platelets and kidney function are watched.
questions.strategy: Match each drug to its test first: warfarin goes with PT/INR, heparin with aPTT, and enoxaparin with neither.

steps.detail: Warfarin and INR; heparin and aPTT plus platelets.
Heparin can lower platelets; enoxaparin is cleared by the kidneys.

elimination.verdict: Several days; INR; platelet count; kidney function.

questions.stem: A patient has pancytopenia on blood counts. The provider now wants to see how crowded the marrow is and how its tissue is arranged. Which procedure gives that information?

options.text: Bone marrow aspiration
options.rationale: Aspiration pulls out liquid marrow for analysis of the cells themselves. A liquid sample cannot show how the tissue is arranged.

options.text: Bone marrow biopsy
options.rationale: A biopsy removes a solid core of tissue, so the lab can judge marrow architecture (how the tissue is arranged) and cellularity (how crowded it is).

options.text: Lymph node biopsy
options.rationale: A lymph node biopsy samples node tissue. It says nothing about the marrow, which is where all three cell lines are made.

options.text: Imaging of the bones
options.rationale: Imaging shows bone, organs and lymph nodes from the outside. It does not give a tissue sample to examine under the microscope.

questions.takeaway: Aspiration takes liquid marrow to look at the cells; biopsy takes a solid core to look at the marrow's structure and cellularity.
questions.strategy: Match the question the provider is asking to the sample. Structure and arrangement need intact tissue, which only a core gives.

steps.detail: Aspiration and biopsy are the two marrow tests; the answer is one of them, so the node biopsy and imaging drop.
Liquid marrow shows cells; a core shows architecture. The stem asks about arrangement and crowding.

elimination.verdict: Bone marrow biopsy is the only option that keeps the tissue intact.

questions.stem: A patient has an enlarged neck lymph node, and a computed tomography (CT) scan shows enlarged chest nodes. Node tissue is needed to find the cause. Which procedure does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Repeat CT imaging with contrast
options.rationale: Imaging has already done its job of showing enlarged nodes. Repeating it still gives no tissue to examine for disease.

options.text: Bone marrow aspiration
options.rationale: Aspiration samples liquid marrow. It is the right test for a marrow question, not for an enlarged node.

options.text: Bone marrow biopsy
options.rationale: A marrow biopsy gives a core of marrow tissue, not node tissue.

options.text: Lymph node biopsy
options.rationale: A lymph node biopsy removes node tissue by needle or by surgery so the tissue can be examined for disease.

questions.takeaway: Imaging finds and measures abnormal nodes, organs and bone; a lymph node biopsy (needle or surgical) gives the tissue that names the cause.
questions.strategy: Ask what the next answer needs. The question is about node tissue, so the sample must come from the node.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Aspiration and biopsy of the marrow both sample the wrong tissue, so they fall together.
Imaging has already shown the nodes; it cannot provide tissue.

elimination.verdict: Lymph node biopsy is the only option that samples the node itself.

questions.stem: A patient scheduled for a bone marrow aspiration with local anesthetic asks, "What am I going to feel?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "You will be asleep and will not feel anything."
options.rationale: A local anesthetic numbs the skin and bone surface only; the patient is awake. Promising no sensation sets the patient up to feel misled.

options.text: "The numbing medicine blocks every sensation completely."
options.rationale: Local anesthetic does not reach the marrow, so pressure and a brief pull are still felt. This is an absolute that is not true.

options.text: "A sting, then pressure and a brief pulling pain."
options.rationale: The expected sensations are a stinging local anesthetic, heavy pressure as the needle enters, and a brief pulling pain when the liquid marrow is drawn out. Telling the patient ahead of time lowers anxiety and helps the patient hold still.

options.text: "Steady, sharp pain for several hours during the test."
options.rationale: The pulling pain is brief and the procedure itself takes about 30 minutes; hours of sharp pain is not expected and frightens the patient needlessly.

questions.takeaway: Before a marrow test, explain the procedure and the sensations to expect: a sting from the local anesthetic, pressure, and a brief pulling pain during aspiration.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Pick the answer that is honest and specific. A patient who knows what is coming is less anxious and more able to stay still.

steps.detail: "Not feel anything" and "blocks every sensation" are both false reassurance.
Hours of sharp pain overstates a brief pull during a 30 minute procedure.

elimination.verdict: The sting, pressure and brief pull is the accurate preparation.

questions.objective: Understand nursing care before and after bone marrow tests

questions.stem: During the preprocedure review for a bone marrow biopsy tomorrow, a patient lists warfarin, a daily fish oil capsule and a sulfa allergy. Which action by the nurse fits the preprocedure review?

options.text: Report the medications and allergy to the provider
options.rationale: Before the procedure the nurse reviews medications, allergies and bleeding risks. Warfarin and fish oil both raise bleeding risk, so the provider decides whether anything is held.

options.text: Tell the patient to skip tonight's warfarin dose
options.rationale: Holding an anticoagulant is a provider decision. The nurse asks whether it is held rather than stopping it on the nurse's own judgment.

options.text: Tell the patient that supplements do not matter
options.rationale: Fish oil can add to bleeding risk; supplements are part of the medication review.

options.text: Plan to give aspirin for discomfort afterward
options.rationale: Aspirin blocks platelet function and adds to bleeding risk; an aspirin free analgesic is used after a marrow test.

questions.takeaway: Before a marrow test, review medications, supplements, allergies and bleeding risks, and ask the provider whether anticoagulants are held.
questions.strategy: Separate what the nurse gathers and reports from what the provider decides. Stopping a drug is a provider order.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Skipping warfarin on the nurse's say so is outside nursing scope.
Dismissing fish oil and planning aspirin both ignore bleeding risk.

elimination.verdict: Reporting the drugs and allergy for a provider decision is the correct review step.

questions.stem: Before giving the ordered sedative for a bone marrow biopsy, the nurse finds that the informed consent form has not been signed. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Give the sedative, then have the patient sign
options.rationale: A sedated patient cannot give valid consent. Consent must come before anything that clouds judgment.

options.text: Explain the risks and have the patient sign
options.rationale: Explaining the procedure's risks and alternatives belongs to the provider who performs it. The nurse confirms consent and may witness the signature, but does not obtain it.

options.text: Ask a family member to sign instead
options.rationale: An alert adult who can make decisions gives consent personally; a family member is not the substitute here.

options.text: Hold the sedative and notify the provider
options.rationale: Confirming informed consent is a before step. Without it, the nurse holds the sedative and lets the provider obtain consent first.

questions.takeaway: Confirm informed consent before the procedure and before any sedation; if it is missing, hold the sedation and notify the provider.
questions.strategy: Ask what makes the next step legal and safe. Once a sedative is in, valid consent is no longer possible.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sedating first and signing after reverses the required order.
Obtaining consent and finding a substitute signer are not the nurse's roles here.

elimination.verdict: Holding the sedative and notifying the provider protects the patient and the consent process.

questions.stem: A bone marrow aspiration will be done at the posterior iliac crest. How does the nurse position the patient?

options.text: Supine with the head of the bed raised
options.rationale: Lying on the back puts the posterior iliac crest against the mattress, where it cannot be reached.

options.text: Prone or side lying
options.rationale: The usual site is the iliac crest, and prone or side lying exposes it while letting the patient stay still and supported.

options.text: Sitting and leaning forward over a table
options.rationale: Leaning over a table is the classic position for a thoracentesis, not for an iliac crest marrow test.

options.text: Supine with a rolled towel under the shoulders
options.rationale: That position exposes the sternum, an alternate marrow site. It does not expose the posterior iliac crest.

questions.takeaway: The usual marrow site is the iliac crest, and the patient lies prone or side lying.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Picture where the needle goes. The posterior hip must face up or out, which only prone or side lying does.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Supine hides the posterior crest; Trendelenburg does nothing for it.
Leaning forward over a table belongs to a different procedure.

elimination.verdict: Prone or side lying is correct.

questions.stem: A patient is in recovery after a bone marrow aspiration and biopsy done with moderate sedation. Which actions does the nurse include in the after care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Leave the dressing unchecked until discharge
options.rationale: The dressing is assessed regularly; a soaked dressing is the early sign of bleeding.

options.text: Apply pressure to the puncture site
options.rationale: Pressure on the site is the first after step and limits bleeding from the bone and skin puncture.

options.text: Check vital signs only if pain increases
options.rationale: After sedation, vital signs follow the sedation recovery protocol on a schedule, not only when pain changes.

options.text: Monitor the site for bleeding, swelling and pain
options.rationale: Bleeding, swelling and pain at the site are the local complications to watch, with bleeding the priority.

options.text: Follow the sedation recovery protocol and vital signs
options.rationale: Sedation can depress breathing and blood pressure, so the patient is monitored per protocol until recovered.

options.text: Teach site care and activity limits before discharge
options.rationale: Site care instructions and activity restrictions are given before the patient goes home.

questions.takeaway: After a marrow test: apply pressure and check the dressing; monitor for bleeding, swelling and pain; follow sedation recovery and vital signs; teach site care and activity limits before discharge.
questions.strategy: Group the after care into four jobs: pressure and dressing, local site checks, sedation recovery, discharge teaching. Any option that skips or delays one of them is wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: "Unchecked until discharge" and "only if pain increases" both limit monitoring that must be regular.
The remaining four match the four after care jobs.

elimination.verdict: Pressure, site monitoring, sedation recovery and discharge teaching are all correct.

questions.stem: One hour after an iliac crest bone marrow biopsy, a patient with platelets of 58 K/µL reports soreness of 3 of 10 and asks about results. Which problem is the monitoring priority?

options.text: Bleeding at the puncture site
options.rationale: Bleeding is the priority after a marrow test, and a low platelet count makes it more likely. It is the complication that can turn dangerous fastest.

options.text: Infection at the puncture site
options.rationale: Infection matters, but it develops over days. It is not the most immediate risk in the first hours.

options.text: Pain at the puncture site
options.rationale: Mild soreness is expected after the procedure and is treated with an aspirin free analgesic; it is not the greatest risk.

options.text: Anxiety about the results
options.rationale: Anxiety is real and deserves attention, but it is a psychosocial need that ranks below a physical safety risk.

questions.takeaway: After a bone marrow aspiration or biopsy, bleeding is the priority, especially when platelets are low.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Rank the problems by how fast each can harm the patient. A physical risk that is active now beats a later risk, an expected finding and an emotional need.

steps.detail: Soreness of 3 of 10 is expected; anxiety is psychosocial.
Infection appears later; bleeding can start right away, and the low platelet count is the cue.

questions.stem: A patient is going home three hours after a bone marrow aspiration. The site is sore, and the patient plays recreational soccer. Which patient statement shows the discharge teaching was understood?

options.text: "I can take aspirin tonight for the soreness."
options.rationale: Aspirin blocks platelet function and raises the risk of bleeding from the site. An aspirin free analgesic is used instead.

options.text: "I can play in my soccer game with the team tomorrow."
options.rationale: The site is protected from injury for 48 hours, so contact sports the next day are too soon.

options.text: "I will check the site every 2 hours for 24 hours."
options.rationale: Checking the site every 2 hours for the first 24 hours catches bleeding or swelling early, which is the main risk after a marrow test.

options.text: "I only need to call if I get a fever."
options.rationale: Bleeding, swelling and warmth at the site are all reasons to call; fever is not the only one, and bleeding is the most urgent.

questions.takeaway: Discharge teaching after a marrow test: check the site every 2 hours for 24 hours, avoid injuring it for 48 hours, use an aspirin free analgesic, and report bleeding, swelling or warmth.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Test each statement against the bleeding risk. Anything that adds bleeding risk, injures the site early, or narrows what to report is a teaching gap.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Aspirin and next day soccer both raise bleeding risk.
"Only" a fever leaves out bleeding and swelling.

elimination.verdict: Checking the site every 2 hours for 24 hours shows understanding.

questions.objective: Understand nursing care before and after bone marrow tests

questions.stem: After a bone marrow aspiration, the nurse is caring for the patient and needs the specimen delivered to the lab. Which task can the nurse assign to the assistive personnel (AP)?

options.text: Checking the puncture site for any bleeding
options.rationale: Assessing the site for bleeding is an assessment and stays with the nurse.

options.text: Deciding whether the dressing needs reinforcing
options.rationale: Judging a dressing and deciding to reinforce it requires nursing judgment.

options.text: Monitoring the patient's recovery from sedation
options.rationale: Sedation recovery needs ongoing assessment of breathing and level of consciousness, which the nurse keeps.

options.text: Taking the labeled specimen to the lab
options.rationale: Transporting a labeled specimen is a routine task with no assessment, so the AP can do it while the nurse stays with the patient.

questions.takeaway: The AP can take the specimen to the lab; assessing the site and the patient's recovery stays with the nurse.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask whether the task needs assessment or judgment. If it does, it stays with the nurse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Checking the site, judging the dressing and watching sedation recovery all require assessment.
Carrying a specimen involves no judgment about the patient.

elimination.verdict: Taking the specimen to the lab is the task the AP can do.

questions.stem: A patient with anemia lives in a house built in the 1950s and spends weekends in the garage sanding old paint off furniture. Which test does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: CBC with differential
options.rationale: A CBC confirms and describes the anemia, but it cannot show what is causing it.

options.text: Blood lead test
options.rationale: Disturbing older paint creates lead dust. Lead interferes with heme production and can contribute to anemia, so a suspected exposure calls for a blood lead test.

options.text: Carboxyhemoglobin level
options.rationale: Carboxyhemoglobin measures carbon monoxide bound to hemoglobin. Nothing in this history points to a combustion source.

options.text: Bone marrow aspiration
options.rationale: A marrow test looks for a problem inside the marrow. It is invasive and does not identify an environmental lead exposure.

questions.takeaway: Old paint, renovation dust and contaminated soil are common lead sources; suspected exposure calls for a blood lead test.
questions.strategy: Link the source in the history to the toxin, then to the test that measures that toxin.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The CBC describes the anemia but not its cause.
Old paint means lead, not carbon monoxide, and lead is measured in the blood, not the marrow.

elimination.verdict: The blood lead test is the one that checks the exposure.

questions.objective: Identify environmental exposures affecting blood health

questions.stem: The nurse is taking an exposure history from a patient with unexplained anemia. Which history findings suggest a risk of lead exposure? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pumps gasoline at a service station
options.rationale: Gasoline points to benzene, which harms the marrow. Lead is not the exposure from modern gasoline.

options.text: Heats the home with a generator in the garage
options.rationale: A generator indoors points to carbon monoxide, which blocks hemoglobin from carrying oxygen.

options.text: Recently removed old paint while renovating
options.rationale: Disturbing older paint during renovation is a classic lead source.

options.text: Smokes a pack of cigarettes a day
options.rationale: Cigarette smoke is a benzene source on the exposure list, not a lead source.

options.text: Grows vegetables in contaminated garden soil
options.rationale: Contaminated dust or soil is a lead source; paint and soil are common local sources.

options.text: Does metalworking as a hobby
options.rationale: Construction, metalworking and hobby activities can expose a person to lead.

questions.takeaway: Lead comes from older paint disturbed during renovation, contaminated dust or soil, and construction, metalworking or hobby activities.
questions.strategy: Sort every history item by its toxin: paint, soil, dust and metal mean lead; gasoline, emissions and smoke mean benzene; fuel burning indoors means carbon monoxide.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Gasoline and cigarette smoke are benzene sources.
A generator in the garage is a carbon monoxide source.

elimination.verdict: Old paint, contaminated soil and metalworking are the lead risks.

questions.objective: Identify environmental exposures affecting blood health

questions.stem: A patient has refueled trucks at a fuel depot for 20 years and lives beside a refinery. Red cells, white cells and platelets are all low. Which explanation links history and results?

options.text: Benzene disrupting marrow blood cell production
options.rationale: Benzene in gasoline and industrial emissions is absorbed and metabolized, then disrupts hematopoiesis. Because the marrow makes all three lines, all three counts fall.

options.text: Lead from fuel blocking heme production
options.rationale: Lead interferes with heme and mainly causes anemia. It would not explain low WBCs and platelets, and current fuel is not the lead source.

options.text: Carbon monoxide binding to hemoglobin
options.rationale: Carbon monoxide stops hemoglobin from carrying oxygen, but it does not lower the number of cells in any line.

options.text: Fuel fumes destroying cells in the spleen
options.rationale: The spleen removes aging cells; fuel fumes are not described as destroying cells there. The problem is production, not removal.

questions.takeaway: Benzene, found in gasoline, industrial emissions, cigarette smoke and some chemical products, disrupts hematopoiesis in the marrow and can lower every cell line.
questions.strategy: Let the lab pattern point to the organ: all three lines low means the marrow, and the toxin that harms the marrow is benzene.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Low counts in all three lines is a marrow production problem.
Lead mainly affects heme and red cells; carbon monoxide affects hemoglobin's job, not cell numbers.

elimination.verdict: Benzene harming the marrow is the explanation that covers every low count.

questions.objective: Identify environmental exposures affecting blood health

questions.stem: A patient's anemia has no clear cause after the first labs. Which question best assesses whether something in the patient's surroundings could be harming the blood?

options.text: "Has anyone in your family had a bleeding disorder?"
options.rationale: Family history is a valid hematologic history item, but it looks for an inherited cause, not an environmental one.

options.text: "How much alcohol do you drink in a week?"
options.rationale: Alcohol use is part of the history, but it is one habit and does not survey the patient's environment.

options.text: "Tell me about your work, home and hobbies."
options.rationale: Asking about home, work and hobby exposures is how the nurse finds lead, benzene or carbon monoxide sources that blood tests alone will not reveal.

options.text: "Do you take iron or other supplements?"
options.rationale: Supplements are part of the medication review. This question does not ask about environmental exposure.

questions.takeaway: Include home, work and hobby exposures in every hematologic history, because some blood problems have an environmental cause that testing alone will not reveal.
questions.strategy: All four questions belong in a hematologic history. Choose the one that matches the goal in the stem, the patient's surroundings, and covers it broadly.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Family history, alcohol and supplements are true history items but not environmental ones.
Work, home and hobbies together cover every common exposure source.

elimination.verdict: Asking about work, home and hobbies is the best exposure question.

questions.objective: Identify environmental exposures affecting blood health

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing exposure histories at a community clinic. For each exposure, indicate how it harms the blood.
questions.scenario: The nurse is reviewing exposure histories for several patients seen in a community clinic.
columns: Disrupts cell production in the marrow

rows.text: Sands old paint while renovating an older home
rows.rationale: Older paint is a lead source, and lead interferes with heme production, which can lead to anemia.

rows.text: Runs a charcoal grill indoors during a power outage
rows.rationale: Burning fuel indoors releases carbon monoxide, which binds hemoglobin and reduces oxygen carrying capacity.

rows.text: Works daily near refinery emissions
rows.answer: Disrupts cell production in the marrow
rows.rationale: Industrial emissions contain benzene, which disrupts hematopoiesis in the marrow.

rows.text: Uses benzene containing solvents at a chemical plant
rows.answer: Disrupts cell production in the marrow
rows.rationale: Some chemical products contain benzene, which harms the marrow's blood cell production.

rows.text: Grows food in contaminated garden soil
rows.rationale: Contaminated soil is a common lead source; lead disrupts heme production.

rows.text: Lives with a faulty furnace and no CO alarm
rows.rationale: A faulty furnace can leak carbon monoxide; without an alarm, exposure goes unnoticed while hemoglobin is blocked from carrying oxygen.

answer.r3: Disrupts cell production in the marrow
answer.r4: Disrupts cell production in the marrow

questions.takeaway: Lead impairs hemoglobin production (heme), benzene harms the marrow, and carbon monoxide impairs hemoglobin function.
questions.strategy: Name the toxin first from the source, then attach its target: lead hits the heme factory, benzene hits the bone marrow, carbon monoxide hits hemoglobin's job.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Paint and soil mean lead; emissions and solvents mean benzene; indoor burning and a faulty furnace mean carbon monoxide.
Lead to heme, benzene to marrow, carbon monoxide to hemoglobin function.

elimination.verdict: Each source maps to one toxin and one way of harming the blood.

questions.objective: Identify environmental exposures affecting blood health

questions.stem: After a night in a generator heated house, a patient has a hemoglobin of 14.2 g/dL and a normal red blood cell count, yet tissues lack oxygen. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: The marrow has stopped making new red cells
options.rationale: A marrow production problem would lower the counts, and these counts are normal.

options.text: Carbon monoxide has taken oxygen's place on hemoglobin
options.rationale: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin far more tightly than oxygen does, forming carboxyhemoglobin. The hemoglobin is present but cannot do its job, so oxygen carrying capacity drops.

options.text: The heme in hemoglobin is being made incorrectly
options.rationale: Faulty heme production describes lead, which tends to cause anemia, not a normal hemoglobin with poor oxygen delivery.

options.text: Red cells are breaking apart in the bloodstream
options.rationale: Red cell destruction would lower the hemoglobin and RBC count over time; carbon monoxide does not work this way.

questions.takeaway: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin and reduces oxygen carrying capacity, so oxygen transport fails even when the RBC count and hemoglobin are normal.
questions.strategy: A normal count with failed oxygen delivery means the problem is the hemoglobin's function, not the number of cells.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Marrow failure and red cell destruction would both lower the counts.
Lead affects how heme is made; carbon monoxide affects what hemoglobin carries.

elimination.verdict: Carbon monoxide occupying hemoglobin explains normal counts with poor oxygen delivery.

questions.objective: Recognize carbon monoxide poisoning and nursing priorities

questions.stem: A patient comes to the clinic in winter. The patient's household has been using a gas space heater with the windows closed, and the patient's partner has felt unwell too. Which findings are consistent with carbon monoxide poisoning? Select all that apply.

options.text: Petechiae on the lower legs
options.rationale: Petechiae point to a platelet problem. Carbon monoxide affects oxygen transport, not clotting.

options.text: Throbbing headache
options.rationale: Headache is one of the most common early signs, from the brain receiving less oxygen.

options.text: Low pulse oximetry value
options.rationale: Pulse oximetry often reads normal in carbon monoxide poisoning because the device cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin. A low value is not expected and its absence rules nothing out.

options.text: New confusion
options.rationale: Confusion reflects the brain not getting enough oxygen and signals a more serious exposure.

options.text: Chest pain
options.rationale: Chest pain occurs because the heart muscle is not getting enough oxygen.

options.text: Partner with the same symptoms
options.rationale: Several people in the same home with the same symptoms, or symptoms that improve away from home, is the key clue.

questions.takeaway: Carbon monoxide poisoning causes headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion and chest pain; several people in the same home with the same symptoms is the clue, and pulse oximetry can read falsely normal.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Ask which findings come from tissues starved of oxygen, and which come from the household pattern. Anything that depends on clotting or on a low oximeter value does not fit.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Headache, confusion and chest pain all come from too little oxygen reaching the brain and heart.
Petechiae belong to platelets; a low oximeter value is not expected.

elimination.verdict: Headache, confusion, chest pain and a partner with the same symptoms are consistent with carbon monoxide poisoning.

questions.objective: Recognize carbon monoxide poisoning and nursing priorities

questions.stem: Three members of one household have headaches that fade at work and return each evening at home. One has an SpO2 of 99% on room air. Which test confirms the suspected problem?

options.text: Repeat pulse oximetry on another finger
options.rationale: Pulse oximetry cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, so it can read falsely normal no matter which finger is used.

options.text: CBC with hemoglobin level
options.rationale: The hemoglobin can be normal in carbon monoxide poisoning because the problem is hemoglobin's function, not its amount.

options.text: Blood lead test
options.rationale: A blood lead test checks lead exposure, which causes anemia over time, not headaches that clear when the household leaves home.

options.text: Carboxyhemoglobin level
options.rationale: A carboxyhemoglobin level measures how much hemoglobin is bound to carbon monoxide and confirms the diagnosis.

questions.takeaway: Suspect carbon monoxide when several people in one home have symptoms that improve away from home; pulse oximetry can read falsely normal, and a carboxyhemoglobin level confirms it.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Do not let a normal SpO2 close the question. Choose the test that measures the toxin directly.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Repeating a test that cannot detect carboxyhemoglobin adds nothing.
Hemoglobin can be normal; the lead test checks a different toxin.

elimination.verdict: The carboxyhemoglobin level confirms carbon monoxide poisoning.

questions.objective: Recognize carbon monoxide poisoning and nursing priorities

questions.stem: A patient is brought to the emergency department with headache, nausea and dizziness after running a portable generator in an attached garage. The SpO2 is 98% on room air. Which actions are appropriate nursing priorities? Select all that apply.

options.text: Titrate oxygen to keep the SpO2 at 94%
options.rationale: The SpO2 can read falsely normal, so it cannot guide oxygen here. Oxygen is not lowered because the oximeter looks good.

options.text: Make sure the patient is away from the source
options.rationale: Removing the patient from the source, with scene safety first, stops further exposure.

options.text: Give 100% oxygen by nonrebreather mask
options.rationale: High flow 100% oxygen by nonrebreather speeds the release of carbon monoxide from hemoglobin and is given right away.

options.text: Assess airway, breathing and neuro status
options.rationale: Carbon monoxide can cause confusion, seizures and loss of consciousness, so airway, breathing and neuro status are watched closely.

options.text: Teach the household to install CO alarms
options.rationale: A working CO alarm warns of exposure before symptoms start and prevents a repeat event.

options.text: Teach the household to keep generators outdoors
options.rationale: Generators and grills are never run indoors or in an attached garage, because the exhaust fills the living space.

questions.takeaway: For carbon monoxide poisoning: remove the patient from the source, give 100% oxygen by nonrebreather, assess airway, breathing and neuro status, and teach CO alarms and no generators indoors.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Treat the SpO2 as unreliable, then work through remove, oxygen, assess, prevent.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Titrating oxygen to an SpO2 that reads falsely normal undertreats the patient.
Remove from the source, give 100% oxygen, assess the airway and brain, then teach prevention.

elimination.verdict: Every option except titrating to the SpO2 is a correct priority.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient having a bone marrow aspiration and biopsy. For each nursing action, indicate whether it belongs before or after the procedure.
questions.scenario: A patient is scheduled for a bone marrow aspiration and biopsy at the posterior iliac crest with sedation.

rows.text: Confirm that informed consent was obtained
rows.rationale: Consent is confirmed before sedation and before the procedure begins.

rows.text: Apply pressure to the site and check the dressing regularly
rows.rationale: Pressure and dressing checks prevent and detect bleeding, the priority after the procedure.

rows.text: Follow sedation recovery protocols and monitor vital signs
rows.rationale: Recovery from sedation is monitored once the procedure is done.

rows.text: Review medications, allergies and bleeding risks
rows.rationale: Anticoagulants, allergies and bleeding risks are reviewed beforehand so the provider can decide what to hold.

rows.text: Explain the pressure and brief pulling pain the patient will feel
rows.rationale: Explaining expected sensations ahead of time lowers anxiety and is part of preparation.

rows.text: Teach site care and activity limits
rows.rationale: Site care and activity restrictions are taught before discharge, after the procedure.

questions.takeaway: Before: explain sensations, confirm consent, review medications and bleeding risks, prepare positioning and sedation. After: pressure and dressing checks, watch for bleeding, swelling and pain, sedation recovery, and discharge teaching.
questions.strategy: Sort by timing: anything that prepares the patient or makes the procedure safe to start is before; anything that protects the site or recovers the patient is after.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Preparation and safety checks come before; site protection and recovery come after.
Consent, review and explanation are before; pressure, sedation recovery and teaching are after.

questions.stem: A patient with a platelet count of 31 K/µL calls because a nosebleed has lasted 25 minutes despite pinching, and the gums bled after brushing. How does the nurse interpret these findings?

options.text: Early signs of anemia from low red cells
options.rationale: Anemia shows as fatigue, pallor and dyspnea. Bleeding from the nose and gums points to platelets.

options.text: Signs of a venous clot forming in the head
options.rationale: A venous clot shows as new limb swelling or pain. These findings are bleeding, the opposite problem.

options.text: Mucosal bleeding typical of a platelet disorder
options.rationale: Epistaxis and gum (gingival) bleeding are mouth and nose signs of a platelet problem. Low platelets show first in small vessels of the nose, gums and skin.

options.text: Expected nasal dryness that does not relate to platelets
options.rationale: Dry air can cause a brief nosebleed, but a 25 minute bleed with gum bleeding and a low platelet count is a bleeding sign.

questions.takeaway: Gum bleeding and epistaxis are mouth and nose signs of a platelet disorder, along with petechiae and bruising.
questions.strategy: Group the findings: both are bleeding from small vessels in a patient with low platelets.

steps.detail: Epistaxis and gingival bleeding.
Small vessel bleeding points to platelets.

questions.stem: A patient asks why a blood transfusion only helps for a few months before another is needed. Which fact about red blood cells explains this?

options.text: Red cells are filtered out by the kidneys each week
options.rationale: The kidney makes erythropoietin; old red cells are removed by the spleen and liver.

options.text: Red cells live about 120 days before they are removed
options.rationale: Mature red cells circulate about 120 days; aging cells become fragile and are destroyed in the spleen and liver, so transfused cells are replaced over months.

options.text: Red cells live about 10 days before they are removed
options.rationale: This is closer to the life span of platelets, not red cells.

options.text: Red cells divide in the bloodstream to replace themselves
options.rationale: Mature red cells have no nucleus and cannot divide; new cells come from the marrow.

questions.takeaway: Red cells live about 120 days. Old cells are destroyed in the spleen and liver, and their iron is recycled.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Recall the red cell life span and where old cells go.

steps.detail: About 120 days.
No nucleus, so no division; removal is by the spleen and liver.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic heavy menstrual bleeding has a low hemoglobin. The nurse reviews the red cell indices. Which result fits iron deficiency anemia?

options.text: High MCV: large red cells
options.rationale: Large (macrocytic) cells point to vitamin B12 or folic acid deficiency, not iron loss.

options.text: Normal MCV with a high reticulocyte count
options.rationale: Chronic iron loss shrinks the cells, and the marrow cannot keep up without iron, so reticulocytes are not high.

options.text: High MCHC: dark, dense red cells
options.rationale: Iron deficiency lowers the MCHC; the cells are pale (hypochromic).

options.text: Low MCV: small red cells
options.rationale: Iron deficiency makes small (microcytic), pale (hypochromic) red cells, so the MCV is low.

questions.takeaway: MCV is red cell size. Small cells (low MCV) point to iron deficiency; large cells (high MCV) point to B12 or folate deficiency.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Link the cause to cell size: chronic blood loss drains iron, and iron poor cells are small and pale.

steps.detail: Chronic blood loss means iron loss.
Iron deficiency makes small cells.

questions.stem: A patient has followed a vegan diet for 10 years without supplements. The tongue is smooth and beefy red, and the feet tingle. Which red cell result does the nurse expect?

options.text: Normal sized cells with a high platelet count
options.rationale: B12 deficiency enlarges red cells; a high platelet count is not part of this picture.

options.text: Pale cells with a high TIBC
options.rationale: A high TIBC with pale cells fits iron deficiency.

options.text: Large red cells with a high MCV
options.rationale: Vitamin B12 deficiency makes large (macrocytic) red cells. The tongue change and nerve symptoms fit B12 deficiency, which a vegan diet risks without supplements.

options.text: Small red cells with a low MCV
options.rationale: Small cells fit iron deficiency, not B12 deficiency.

questions.takeaway: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes large red cells (high MCV), a smooth beefy red tongue and nerve damage that can become permanent. A vegan diet lacks B12 unless supplemented.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Name the deficiency from the diet and the nerve signs, then recall its cell size.

steps.detail: Vegan diet, tongue change and tingling point to B12.
B12 deficiency makes large cells.

questions.stem: A patient's labs are reported as iron deficiency anemia. Which results fit this diagnosis? Select all that apply.

options.text: Low serum ferritin
options.rationale: Ferritin reflects total iron stores; it is low when stores are used up.

options.text: High total iron binding capacity (TIBC)
options.rationale: TIBC rises in iron deficiency because transferrin has empty sites waiting for iron.

options.text: High serum iron
options.rationale: Serum iron is low in iron deficiency; it is high in hemochromatosis or iron poisoning.

options.text: Low MCV
options.rationale: Iron deficiency makes small red cells.

options.text: High MCHC
options.rationale: The cells are pale (hypochromic), so the MCHC is low.

options.text: Low serum iron
options.rationale: Little iron is circulating when stores are depleted.

questions.takeaway: In iron deficiency, iron, ferritin, MCV and MCHC are low; TIBC is the one value that is high.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Remember the exception: everything about iron is low except TIBC, the empty carrying capacity.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Iron measures and cell size are low.
TIBC is high.

elimination.verdict: Low ferritin, high TIBC, low MCV, low serum iron.

questions.stem: Four days after a large gastrointestinal bleed, a patient's reticulocyte count has risen from 1% to 4%. How does the nurse interpret this?

options.text: The patient is developing an infection
options.rationale: Infection raises the WBC count, not reticulocytes.

options.text: The marrow is responding by releasing young red cells
options.rationale: Reticulocytes are immature red cells. A rise 3 to 4 days after hemorrhage, or during anemia treatment, shows the marrow is answering the loss.

options.text: The bleeding has started again and needs reporting
options.rationale: A rising reticulocyte count reflects new red cell production, not new bleeding. Hemoglobin trend and bleeding signs show rebleeding.

options.text: The marrow is failing to make new red cells
options.rationale: Marrow failure lowers the reticulocyte count; this count is rising.

questions.takeaway: A rising reticulocyte count after bleeding or during anemia treatment is good news: the marrow is making new red cells. A low count means the marrow is not responding.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Know what a reticulocyte is, then ask whether more of them means more production or more loss.

steps.detail: A reticulocyte is a young red cell.
Rising means the marrow is producing.

questions.stem: Twenty minutes into a blood transfusion, a patient develops chills, back pain and dark urine. Which test result would confirm that antibodies are attacking the transfused red cells?

options.text: Elevated D dimer level
options.rationale: D dimer shows a clot is breaking down; it does not show antibodies on red cells.

options.text: Prolonged aPTT
options.rationale: aPTT measures the intrinsic clotting pathway and monitors heparin.

options.text: Low platelet count
options.rationale: A low platelet count shows bleeding risk; it does not detect antibodies against red cells.

options.text: Positive direct Coombs test
options.rationale: The direct Coombs test detects antibodies attached to red cells; a positive result supports a hemolytic transfusion reaction.

questions.takeaway: A positive Coombs test means antibodies are attached to red cells, as in a hemolytic transfusion reaction or autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask which test looks for antibodies on red cells; the others measure clotting.

steps.detail: Antibodies destroying transfused red cells.
Coombs detects antibodies on red cells; the rest are clotting tests.

questions.stem: A trauma patient with type O negative blood needs an emergency transfusion. Which red cells can this patient safely receive?

options.text: Any type, because O is universal
options.rationale: O negative is the universal red cell donor. As a recipient, O negative can receive only O negative.

options.text: AB positive, the universal type
options.rationale: AB positive is the universal recipient, not a safe red cell type for an O negative patient.

options.text: O negative only
options.rationale: An O negative patient has anti A and anti B antibodies and is Rh negative, so only O negative red cells are compatible. O negative is the universal donor, not the universal recipient.

options.text: O negative or O positive
options.rationale: Rh negative patients receive only Rh negative red cells.

questions.takeaway: O negative is the universal red cell donor but can receive only O negative. AB positive is the universal recipient. Rh negative patients receive only Rh negative red cells.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Separate donor from recipient: O negative gives to everyone but takes from no one else.

steps.detail: The patient is the recipient.
Rh negative receives only Rh negative.

questions.stem: The nurse is checking red cell compatibility for four patients. For each pairing, indicate whether the donor red cells are compatible or not compatible.
questions.scenario: The blood bank calls the nurse about red cell units for four patients.

rows.text: AB positive patient receiving A negative red cells
rows.rationale: AB positive is the universal recipient and can receive red cells of any type.

rows.text: A positive patient receiving O negative red cells
rows.rationale: O negative is the universal red cell donor.

rows.text: B negative patient receiving B positive red cells
rows.rationale: An Rh negative patient receives only Rh negative red cells.

rows.text: A negative patient receiving AB negative red cells
rows.rationale: AB cells carry the B antigen, which an A patient's anti B antibodies attack.

rows.text: O positive patient receiving O negative red cells
rows.rationale: An O positive patient can receive O positive or O negative red cells.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

Rh negative receives only Rh negative.

questions.stem: An 86 year old patient has a productive cough, crackles and new confusion. The white blood cell count is 9,000/mm3. What explains a WBC count that is not elevated?

options.text: The lab result is likely an error to be redrawn
options.rationale: Nothing suggests an error; the value fits a blunted response with aging.

options.text: Aging can blunt the WBC rise with infection
options.rationale: With aging, lymphocytes react less and the WBC count may not rise as much, so a normal count does not rule out infection.

options.text: A normal WBC count rules out a bacterial infection
options.rationale: This is the trap: in older adults a normal count can coexist with infection.

options.text: The confusion is from aging, not infection
options.rationale: New confusion is a change from baseline and is often the first sign of infection in an older adult.

questions.takeaway: In older adults the WBC count may not rise with infection. Rely on other cues, such as new confusion, fever trend and focal signs.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Do not let one normal number override the clinical picture in an older adult.

steps.detail: Cough, crackles and new confusion suggest infection.
Aging blunts the WBC rise.

questions.stem: Three weeks after a Johnson & Johnson COVID vaccine, a patient reports a severe headache, leg swelling and new bruising. Platelets are 48 K/µL. What does the nurse do?

options.rationale: Waiting delays treatment of a condition that can be fatal.

options.text: Give a heparin dose for the leg swelling
options.rationale: VITT is treated with IV immunoglobulin and a nonheparin anticoagulant; heparin is avoided.

options.text: Apply ice and elevate the leg
options.rationale: Comfort measures do not address a possible clot with low platelets.

options.text: Report the findings to the provider right away

questions.strategy: Recognize the pairing of clot signs with low platelets after the vaccine window, then pick the action that does not delay care.

Report right away.

questions.stem: A patient will have a bone scan to look for bone changes from multiple myeloma and plans to fly home 2 days later. Which teaching is accurate?

options.text: Fast for 12 hours and stay in bed after the scan
options.rationale: Fasting or bed rest is needed after a bone scan.

options.text: The tracer may set off airport screening for several days
options.rationale: Radioactive tracer can be detected for several days; give the patient documentation of the scan.

options.text: Avoid drinking fluids for 24 hours after the scan
options.rationale: The patient is encouraged to drink water to help eliminate the tracer.

options.text: Stay away from other people for 1 week
options.rationale: Isolation is needed; the tracer leaves within hours.

questions.stem: A patient started on warfarin for a deep vein clot in the calf asks, "Will this medicine dissolve the clot?" Which statement about anticoagulants is accurate?

options.text: They break down clots that have already formed in the vein
options.rationale: This describes fibrinolytics, not anticoagulants.

options.text: They work by destroying platelets in the blood
options.rationale: Anticoagulants act on clotting factors; they do not destroy platelets.

options.text: They prevent new clots but do not dissolve existing clots
options.rationale: Anticoagulants block steps of the cascade to stop new clots and clot growth. Only fibrinolytics such as alteplase break down a formed clot.

options.text: They thin the blood so it flows more easily
options.rationale: Patients call them blood thinners, but anticoagulants do not change blood viscosity.

questions.takeaway: Anticoagulants prevent new clots and clot growth but do not dissolve existing clots or thin the blood. Fibrinolytics break down formed clots.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Separate preventing a clot from breaking one down.

steps.detail: Prevents formation and growth.
Dissolving clots is a different drug class.

elimination.verdict: They prevent new clots but do not dissolve existing ones.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a 78 year old patient at a clinic visit. Which statement by the patient requires follow up?

options.text: My hair has been thinning slowly on my legs for years
options.rationale: Slow, even hair loss on the legs is a normal aging change.

options.text: My skin gets drier in the winter
options.rationale: Dry skin is common in older adults and is not a reliable sign of a blood problem.

options.text: I bruise more easily now that I am older
options.rationale: New or easier bruising is a bleeding tendency to evaluate, not an aging change. Compare with the patient's baseline and assess for a platelet or clotting problem.

options.text: I have had the same energy level as last year
options.rationale: Energy that matches the patient's own baseline is reassuring, not a finding to follow up.

questions.takeaway: Unexplained or easier bruising in an older adult is evaluated, not explained away by age. Slow leg hair loss and dry skin are expected.
questions.strategy: Find the statement that describes a change in bruising, bleeding, energy or infections; the patient's own explanation of aging does not make it normal.

steps.detail: Leg hair thinning and dry skin fit aging.
Easier bruising is a new bleeding tendency.

questions.objective: Recognize hematologic abnormalities from assessments

questions.stem: A patient receiving chemotherapy has a platelet count of 22 K/µL this morning. The nurse reviews the note below. Highlight the findings that require follow up.
questions.nursesNote: 0800. Alert and oriented. Pinpoint red spots scattered on both lower legs. Gums bleed when brushing teeth. Temperature 36.9 °C. Heart rate 84/min. Reports a new headache since last night, 7 of 10. Pink tinged urine in the urinal. Skin warm and dry. Ate 75% of breakfast.

segments.rationale: Normal mental status is reassuring. A change such as confusion would need follow up because it can signal bleeding in the brain.

segments.text: Pinpoint red spots scattered on both lower legs
segments.rationale: These are petechiae, tiny bleeds in the smallest vessels. They are a classic sign that platelets are too low to plug small vessel injuries.
Gum bleeding is mucous membrane bleeding from thrombocytopenia. It needs follow up and bleeding precautions.
This temperature is normal and does not need follow up right now.
A heart rate of 84/min is within normal limits. Tachycardia would suggest blood loss or anemia.

segments.text: Reports a new headache since last night, 7 of 10
segments.rationale: A new, severe headache in a patient with very low platelets can signal bleeding inside the skull. It is the most urgent finding in the note and is reported right away.

segments.text: Pink tinged urine in the urinal
segments.rationale: Pink urine suggests hematuria, which is bleeding from the urinary tract caused by low platelets.
Warm, dry skin is a normal finding.
Good intake is reassuring and is not a sign of bleeding.

questions.takeaway: Low platelets show first as bleeding in small vessels and mucous membranes: petechiae, gum bleeding and hematuria. A new headache can mean bleeding in the brain and is reported right away.
questions.strategy: With a low platelet count, scan the note for any sign of bleeding in any system: skin, mouth, urine, stool and the brain.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask one question of each finding
steps.detail: Is this a sign of bleeding or a change from normal?
Petechiae, gum bleeding, pink urine and a new severe headache all point to bleeding.
Normal temperature, heart rate, skin, intake and orientation need no follow up.

elimination.verdict: Highlight the petechiae, gum bleeding, new headache and pink tinged urine.

questions.objective: Recognize hematologic abnormalities from assessments

questions.stem: The nurse receives morning results for four patients. Which patient does the nurse assess first?

options.text: Taking warfarin, INR 2.6, no bleeding noted
options.rationale: An INR of 2.6 is within the usual warfarin goal of 2 to 3, and there is no bleeding. This result is therapeutic and expected.

options.text: Neutrophils low after chemotherapy, temperature 38.4 °C
options.rationale: Neutropenia carries the highest infection risk, and a fever here can mean a fast moving infection the body cannot fight. This is the unstable patient and is seen first.

options.text: Heparin infusion, aPTT twice the control value
options.rationale: An aPTT about 1.5 to 2.5 times the control value is the usual therapeutic range for unfractionated heparin. This result is on target.

options.text: Enoxaparin daily, no aPTT ordered this week
options.rationale: Enoxaparin usually needs no routine clotting test, and the aPTT does not measure its effect. No aPTT is expected, not a problem.

questions.takeaway: Neutropenia carries the highest infection risk, so a fever in a neutropenic patient is urgent. Therapeutic INR and aPTT values are expected findings.
questions.strategy: Sort each patient as expected or unexpected. Three results are on target for their drug; only one shows a new problem in a high risk patient.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Check each lab against its drug
steps.detail: INR 2.6 on warfarin and aPTT twice control on heparin are both therapeutic.
No aPTT for enoxaparin is the expected plan, not an omission.
Only the neutropenic patient has a new abnormal finding: fever.

elimination.verdict: Assess the neutropenic patient with a fever first.

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a patient going home on enoxaparin injections. Which patient statements indicate understanding? Select all that apply.

options.text: I will need an INR blood test every week
options.rationale: INR monitors warfarin. Enoxaparin usually needs no routine clotting test, and INR and aPTT do not measure its effect.

options.text: I will report black, tarry stools right away
options.rationale: Black, tarry stool is melena, a sign of GI bleeding. Bleeding is the main risk of any anticoagulant.

options.text: I will cut out leafy green vegetables completely
options.rationale: Vitamin K intake matters for warfarin, and even then the teaching is to keep it consistent, not to cut it out. Enoxaparin works through antithrombin, not vitamin K.

options.text: I will check with my provider before taking ibuprofen
options.rationale: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen can cause GI bleeding and add to anticoagulant bleeding risk.

options.text: I will tell my provider that I take fish oil
options.rationale: Fish oil can increase bleeding, so supplements are part of the medication review.

options.text: I will keep my appointments for platelet count checks
options.rationale: Enoxaparin can lower platelets, so bleeding, platelet counts and kidney function are monitored.

questions.takeaway: Enoxaparin usually needs no routine INR or aPTT; teaching focuses on bleeding signs, avoiding NSAIDs and supplements that add bleeding risk, and platelet checks.
questions.strategy: Sort each statement by which anticoagulant it belongs to. INR checks and vitamin K diet rules belong to warfarin, not enoxaparin.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weekly INR and vitamin K diet changes are warfarin ideas placed on the wrong drug.
Reporting melena, avoiding ibuprofen and reporting fish oil all reduce bleeding risk.
Platelet counts are monitored with enoxaparin.

elimination.verdict: Melena reporting, ibuprofen check, fish oil disclosure and platelet checks show understanding.

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

questions.stem: The nurse is admitting a patient with pancytopenia after chemotherapy. For each finding, indicate the risk it most directly signals.
questions.scenario: A patient with pancytopenia after chemotherapy is admitted. The nurse reviews the admission findings.

rows.text: Platelets 18 K/µL
rows.rationale: A very low platelet count means platelets cannot form the initial plug at vessel injuries, so bleeding risk is high.

rows.text: Petechiae across the chest
rows.rationale: Petechiae are pinpoint bleeds in tiny vessels and are a classic sign of thrombocytopenia.

rows.text: Neutrophils 0.4 K/µL
rows.rationale: Neutropenia carries the highest infection vulnerability because neutrophils are the first responders to bacteria. A count this low means almost no first responders are available.

rows.text: Temperature 38.2 °C with chills
rows.rationale: Fever with chills in a patient with low WBCs signals infection, even if other signs of inflammation are muted.

rows.text: Hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL
rows.rationale: Low hemoglobin means less oxygen carrying protein, so tissues receive less oxygen. This is the anemia part of pancytopenia.

rows.text: Short of breath walking to the bathroom
rows.rationale: Dyspnea and activity intolerance are how anemia shows itself: the heart and lungs work harder to deliver oxygen with too few RBCs.

questions.takeaway: Pancytopenia lowers all three cell lines, so assess for bleeding, infection and poor oxygen delivery at every encounter. Each finding points back to the cell line that is low.
questions.strategy: Link each finding to the cell that is missing: platelets mean bleeding, neutrophils mean infection, RBCs and hemoglobin mean oxygen delivery.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Name the cell line behind each finding
steps.detail: Platelets and petechiae trace to platelets; neutrophils and fever trace to WBCs; hemoglobin and dyspnea trace to RBCs.

steps.action: Match the cell to its job
steps.detail: Platelets plug, neutrophils defend, hemoglobin carries oxygen.

elimination.verdict: Platelet and petechiae findings signal bleeding, neutrophil and fever findings signal infection, and hemoglobin and dyspnea findings signal poor oxygen delivery.

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

questions.stem: Three hours after an iliac crest aspiration, a patient's platelets are 62 K/µL. A quarter size spot on the dressing is larger than 1 hour ago. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Give an aspirin free analgesic
options.rationale: Pain control matters, but the growing spot is active bleeding, which comes first.

options.text: Mark the spot and recheck in 1 hour
options.rationale: Marking helps track drainage, but waiting an hour lets active bleeding continue in a patient with low platelets.

options.text: Change the dressing and assess the site
options.rationale: Removing the dressing disturbs the clot forming at the site and delays pressure.

options.text: Apply firm pressure to the site
options.rationale: Bleeding is the priority after a bone marrow procedure. A growing spot with low platelets is active bleeding, so pressure comes first, then the provider is notified.

questions.takeaway: After a bone marrow aspiration, bleeding is the priority. A growing spot on the dressing means active bleeding: apply firm pressure first.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Spot the active problem (the spot is growing) and choose the action that stops it now.

steps.detail: Growing drainage with low platelets is active bleeding.

steps.action: Pick the action that stops it
steps.detail: Pressure acts now; rechecking and pain relief do not.

elimination.verdict: Apply firm pressure to the site.

questions.objective: Understand nursing care before and after bone marrow tests

questions.stem: A patient is scheduled for a bone marrow aspiration at the posterior iliac crest with sedation this afternoon. Which actions does the nurse include before the procedure? Select all that apply.

options.text: Apply firm pressure to the iliac crest
options.rationale: Pressure is applied after the needle is removed, to control bleeding. It is not a preparation step.

options.text: Position the patient prone or side lying as ordered
options.rationale: Prone or side lying exposes the posterior iliac crest, the usual site.

options.text: Keep the patient NPO as ordered because sedation will be used
options.rationale: Fasting is needed for local anesthetic alone, but when sedation is planned the patient is kept NPO as ordered.

options.text: Ask the provider whether warfarin is to be held
options.rationale: Bleeding risks and anticoagulants are reviewed before the procedure; the provider decides whether to hold them.

options.text: Withhold all fluids for 24 hours beforehand
options.rationale: NPO time follows the sedation order; a 24 hour fluid restriction is not standard and risks dehydration.

options.text: Give aspirin for comfort before the procedure
options.rationale: Aspirin blocks platelets and raises bleeding risk; it is avoided around the procedure.

questions.takeaway: Before a bone marrow aspiration with sedation: position prone or side lying, keep NPO as ordered, and review anticoagulants with the provider. Pressure comes after; aspirin is avoided.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort each option by timing and safety: preparation steps before, site pressure after, and nothing that adds bleeding risk.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pressure is an after step.
Aspirin and a 24 hour fluid restriction are not appropriate.

elimination.verdict: Positioning, NPO as ordered, and asking about warfarin.

questions.objective: Understand nursing care before and after bone marrow tests

questions.stem: A patient with new anemia gives this history. Which detail is most important for the nurse to follow up?

options.text: Eats red meat about once a week
options.rationale: Diet matters for blood health, but eating some red meat weekly is not a strong cause of new anemia and is not an exposure risk.

options.text: Takes a daily multivitamin with iron
options.rationale: A multivitamin with iron supports RBC production. It does not explain the anemia and is not a hazard.

options.text: Cooks on a gas stove with a working CO alarm
options.rationale: Carbon monoxide impairs hemoglobin function but does not lower the hemoglobin count, and a working alarm lowers the risk. This does not explain anemia.

options.text: Has been stripping paint in a 1920s home
options.rationale: Disturbing older paint during renovation is a common source of lead exposure. Lead interferes with heme production and can cause anemia, so the nurse follows up and anticipates a blood lead test.

questions.takeaway: Ask about home, work and hobby exposures in every hematologic history. Old paint disturbed during renovation is a classic lead source, and lead blocks heme production.
questions.strategy: Match the problem to the exposure that causes it. Anemia means less hemoglobin is being made, so look for the exposure that blocks heme production.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A multivitamin with iron and weekly red meat support blood production.
Carbon monoxide blocks hemoglobin function, not production, and the alarm works.
Old paint dust means lead, which lowers heme production and causes anemia.

elimination.verdict: Follow up on the paint stripping in an old home.

questions.objective: Identify environmental exposures affecting blood health

questions.stem: A patient found in a closed garage with a running generator is receiving 100% oxygen by nonrebreather. Which finding most indicates the need for escalation and possible hyperbaric oxygen?

options.text: Headache rated 7 of 10
options.rationale: Headache is the most common symptom of carbon monoxide poisoning; by itself it does not mark severe poisoning.

options.text: Nausea and one episode of vomiting
options.rationale: Nausea and vomiting are common symptoms and do not on their own signal a severe exposure.

options.text: SpO2 of 99% on the nonrebreather
options.rationale: Pulse oximetry can read falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning, so this number neither reassures nor signals severity.

options.text: New confusion that is getting worse
options.rationale: Worsening neurologic status, such as new confusion or loss of consciousness, signals severe poisoning and is escalated promptly; severe cases may need hyperbaric oxygen.

questions.takeaway: In carbon monoxide poisoning, neurologic changes such as new or worsening confusion or loss of consciousness mark severe poisoning and are escalated promptly. A normal SpO2 means nothing here.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Separate common symptoms from signs of severity: the brain is the organ that shows a dangerous oxygen shortage.

steps.detail: SpO2 can read falsely normal with carbon monoxide.
Headache and nausea are common; worsening confusion is a severe sign.

questions.objective: Recognize carbon monoxide poisoning and nursing priorities

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient brought in from a home heated overnight by a kerosene heater. Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the patient is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.
questions.scenario: Three people from one household arrive at the emergency department in winter. They spent the night heating a closed room with a kerosene heater. The patient the nurse is assessing reports a throbbing headache, nausea and dizziness, and the other two have the same headache. Heart rate is 112/min. SpO2 is 98% on room air.

options.text: Give an antiemetic and encourage oral fluids
options.rationale: This treats the nausea as a stomach illness and misses the hypoxia that is causing it.

options.text: Notify the provider and expect a carboxyhemoglobin level
options.rationale: Prompt reporting is a priority, and a carboxyhemoglobin level confirms the diagnosis. Severe cases may need hyperbaric oxygen.

options.text: Give oxygen at 2 L by nasal cannula
options.rationale: Low flow oxygen is too weak to displace carbon monoxide from hemoglobin.

options.text: Titrate oxygen down to an SpO2 of 94%
options.rationale: Pulse oximetry can read falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning, so oxygen is not lowered based on it.

options.text: Apply 100% oxygen by nonrebreather mask
options.rationale: 100% oxygen speeds removal of carbon monoxide from hemoglobin and is given right away, regardless of the SpO2 value.

options.text: Viral gastroenteritis
options.rationale: Household spread and nausea fit, but a throbbing headache shared by everyone and a fuel burning heater in a closed room point to an exposure, not a virus.

options.text: Carbon monoxide poisoning
options.rationale: Headache, nausea and dizziness in several people from one home heated by a fuel burning heater is the classic pattern. The SpO2 is falsely normal.

options.text: Migraine headache
options.rationale: Migraine explains headache and nausea in one person, not the same headache in three people at once.

options.text: Influenza
options.rationale: Winter and a household cluster fit, but there is no fever or body aches, and the closed room with a fuel burning heater points to an exposure.

options.text: Hemoglobin level
options.rationale: The hemoglobin amount is usually normal. The problem is that carbon monoxide is bound to it, not that there is too little of it.

options.text: Carboxyhemoglobin level
options.rationale: This level confirms carbon monoxide poisoning and shows whether treatment is working as it falls.

options.text: Pulse oximetry trend
options.rationale: The oximeter cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, so its values stay falsely normal and do not track recovery.

options.text: Blood lead level
options.rationale: It is another environmental test, but lead causes anemia over months, not overnight symptoms from a heater.

options.text: Neurologic status and level of consciousness
options.rationale: The brain is very sensitive to low oxygen. Confusion, seizures or loss of consciousness signal severe poisoning.

questions.takeaway: Several people from one home with headache, nausea and dizziness near a fuel burning heater means carbon monoxide until proven otherwise. Give 100% oxygen, report promptly, and follow the carboxyhemoglobin level and neuro status, not the SpO2.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Start with the condition: the shared symptoms and the heater make the pattern. Then pick actions and parameters that do not depend on the oximeter.

steps.detail: Same symptoms in several household members with a fuel burning heater points to carbon monoxide.
Titrating to SpO2 and trending SpO2 both trust a falsely normal value.

steps.action: Choose oxygen strength and the right lab
steps.detail: 100% oxygen by nonrebreather and the carboxyhemoglobin level match the problem.

elimination.verdict: Carbon monoxide poisoning: give 100% oxygen by nonrebreather, notify the provider for a carboxyhemoglobin level, and monitor carboxyhemoglobin and neuro status.

questions.objective: Recognize carbon monoxide poisoning and nursing priorities

questions.stem: Fifteen minutes into a unit of packed red blood cells, a patient reports chills and low back pain. Temperature rose from 36.9 °C to 38.3 °C. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Slow the transfusion and recheck vital signs in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Slowing still delivers incompatible cells. Chills, back pain and a fever early in a transfusion suggest a hemolytic reaction, so the transfusion is stopped, not slowed.

options.text: Give acetaminophen and continue the transfusion as ordered
options.rationale: Treating the fever hides the reaction while more incompatible blood is given.

options.text: Stop the transfusion and keep the IV line open
options.rationale: Stopping limits how much incompatible blood enters. Keeping the line open with 0.9% sodium chloride (new tubing) preserves access for treatment; then the provider and blood bank are notified.

options.text: Send a blood sample for a Coombs test before stopping
options.rationale: A Coombs test helps confirm a hemolytic reaction, but testing never comes before stopping the infusion.

questions.takeaway: Signs of a transfusion reaction mean stop the transfusion first, keep the line open with 0.9% sodium chloride, then notify the provider and blood bank. Typing, antibody screen and crossmatch exist to prevent this reaction.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Every option except one keeps the blood running or delays stopping it. In a suspected reaction, the first action removes the cause.

steps.detail: Chills, back pain and fever 15 minutes in suggest a hemolytic reaction.
Stop the blood; tests and comfort measures come after.

elimination.verdict: Stop the transfusion and keep the line open.

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

questions.stem: On heparin day 6, a patient's platelets are 98 K/µL, down from 260 K/µL on admission. The activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) is in the ordered range. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Continue the infusion because the aPTT is therapeutic
options.rationale: A therapeutic aPTT shows the dose is right, but it says nothing about platelets. The drop is a separate safety problem.

options.text: Report the platelet drop to the provider promptly
options.rationale: Heparin can lower the platelet count, which is why platelets are monitored during therapy. A fall of more than half from baseline is reported promptly so the provider can decide whether to stop heparin.

options.text: Increase the infusion rate to prevent new clots
options.rationale: Raising the dose ignores the platelet drop and adds bleeding risk.

options.text: Recheck the platelet count again in 1 week
options.rationale: Waiting a week lets a dangerous drop continue.

questions.takeaway: During heparin therapy, the nurse watches the platelet count as well as the aPTT. A large drop from baseline is reported promptly, even when the aPTT is therapeutic.
questions.strategy: Two labs are given. Decide which one is the problem: the aPTT is in range, the platelets have fallen by more than half.

steps.detail: aPTT in range; platelets fell from 260 to 98.
Heparin requires platelet monitoring.
